Surah al-Anbiya' (The Prophets)

Meccan

* *

﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near for them, yet they turn away heedlessly.﴾ It has been said that the lam here means "from" (min), so the meaning is: their reckoning has drawn near from people, that is, the time of Allah's calling them to account for their deeds, namely the Day of Resurrection. It was revealed concerning those who denied the Resurrection. ﴿And they are heedless, turning away﴾ from preparing for it.

﴿No reminder comes to them from their Lord, newly revealed﴾ means: whatever new portion of the Qur'an Allah sends down, by which He admonishes and exhorts them.

Muqatil said: Allah brings about one matter after another [[addition from (b)]]. It has been said: the "newly revealed reminder" is what the Prophet ﷺ said and explained of the Sunnah and admonitions, apart from the Qur'an. He attributed it to the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, because it was spoken by the command of the Lord. ﴿Except that they listen to it while playing﴾ means they listen to it in play, not taking heed and not being admonished.

﴿Their hearts distracted﴾ means heedless and inattentive, ﴿their hearts﴾ turned away from the remembrance of Allah. His saying ﴿distracted﴾ is an adjective that precedes the noun, and the adjective ought to follow the noun in its i'rab (grammatical case). When an adjective precedes its noun it has two states: fasl (separation) and wasl (connection). Its state in the fasl is the accusative, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿humbled their eyes﴾ (al-Qamar: 7), ﴿and its shade close over them﴾ (al-Insan: 11), and ﴿distracted their hearts﴾. In the wasl, its case follows that of what precedes it, as in His saying: ﴿Bring us out of this town whose people are wrongdoers﴾ (al-Nisa': 75); and ﴿And they conspired secretly, those who did wrong﴾, meaning those who associated partners with Allah. His saying ﴿wa-asarru﴾ ("and they conspired") is a verb that precedes the plural subject, and its correct form would be wa-asarra (singular). Al-Kisa'i said: there is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in it; the intended sense is: "those who did wrong conspired secretly."

It has also been said: the "alladhina" is in the nominative as a new subject (mubtada'), meaning: "And they conspired secretly," then he said: "They are those who did wrong."

It has also been said: it is in the nominative as a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in asarru. Al-Mubarrad said: this is like your saying, "Indeed those who are in the house departed, the sons of 'Abd Allah," as a badal from the subject of "departed." Then He explained their secret which they conspired about, saying: ﴿Is this not but a human like you?﴾ They denied that humans be sent as messengers and demanded that angels be sent.

﴿Will you then come to magic﴾ meaning, will you attend the magic and accept it, ﴿while you see﴾ knowing that it is magic.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 4–6:

Say to them, O Muhammad: ﴿My Lord knows every word in the heaven and the earth﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "Qala Rabbi" (He said, "My Lord"), as a report about Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿He knows every word in the heaven and the earth﴾, meaning nothing is hidden from Him. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of their sayings, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of their deeds.

﴿Rather, they say: "A confusion of dreams"﴾, its falsehoods [and its sayings] [[addition from (b).]] and its frightening illusions, which he saw in sleep. ﴿Rather, he has invented it﴾, fabricated it. ﴿Rather, he is a poet﴾. This means that the polytheists disagreed about the Qur'an and about what he was saying. Some of them said, "A confusion of dreams"; some said, "Rather, it is a fabrication"; and some said, "Rather, Muhammad is a poet, and what he has brought you is poetry."

﴿So let him bring us a sign﴾, Muhammad, ﴿if he is truthful, as the earlier ones were sent with signs﴾ from the messengers. God Most High answered them: ﴿No town before them that We destroyed believed﴾, before the polytheists of Makkah, ﴿of a town﴾, that is, of the people of a town to which the signs came, ﴿We destroyed them﴾ for their denial. ﴿Will they believe?﴾ If a sign comes to them. The meaning is: those earlier people did not believe in the signs when they came to them, so will these people believe?

**The Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 21, Verses 7–10:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed﴾. This is a response to their saying: ﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ That is, We did not send angels to the earlier peoples; rather, We sent men to whom We revealed. ﴿So ask the people of the reminder﴾, that is, the people of the Torah (Tawrat) and the Gospel (Injil), meaning the scholars of the People of the Book, for they do not deny that the messengers were human beings, even though they deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). He commanded the polytheists to ask them because they are closer to affirming one who did not believe in the Prophet (ﷺ) than to affirming one who did believe in him.

Ibn Zayd said: by "the reminder" He meant the Qur'an (See: al-Tabari: 17/5). The meaning is: ask the believing, knowledgeable people among the people of the Qur'an. ﴿If you do not know﴾.

﴿And We did not make them﴾, that is, the messengers, ﴿bodies﴾ (the word is singular, not plural, because it is a noun of genus), ﴿who did not eat food﴾. This is a rebuttal of their saying: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food?﴾ (al-Furqan: 7). The meaning is: We did not make the messengers angels; rather We made them human beings who eat food. ﴿Nor were they immortal﴾ in this world.

﴿Then We fulfilled for them the promise﴾ which We had promised them, of destroying their enemies, ﴿and We saved them and whom We willed﴾, that is, We saved the believers who affirmed them, ﴿and We destroyed the transgressors﴾, that is, the polytheists who denied them. Every polytheist is a transgressor against himself.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book﴾, O assembly of Quraysh, ﴿in which is your reminder﴾, that is, your honor, as He said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 44). It is an honor for whoever believes in it.

Mujahid said: "in it is your story." And al-Hasan said: "in it is your reminder," that is, a reminder of what you need concerning the matter of your religion. ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 11–16:

﴿How many a town have We shattered﴾ — i.e., We destroyed. Al-qasm (shattering) means breaking. ﴿of a town that was wrongdoing﴾ — i.e., disbelieving, meaning its people. ﴿and raised up after it﴾ — i.e., We brought into being after the destruction of its people ﴿another people﴾.

﴿Then when they perceived Our might﴾ — i.e., [saw] [[Addition from (b).]] Our punishment with the sense of sight. ﴿behold, they fled from it, hastening away﴾ — i.e., they hurried off in flight.

﴿Do not flee﴾ — i.e., it was said to them: do not flee, do not run away. ﴿and return to that wherein you were made to live in luxury and your dwellings, that you may be questioned.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: about the killing of your Prophet. Qatadah said: about some of your worldly possessions. This verse was revealed concerning the people of Hasura, which is a town in Yemen whose inhabitants were Arabs. God sent to them a prophet calling them to God, but they denied him and killed him, so God set Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) over them until he killed them and took them captive. [[See: al-Tabari: 17/9.]] When the killing continued among them, they regretted, fled and were routed. Then the angels said to them in mockery: Do not flee, and return to your dwellings and your wealth, that you may be questioned.

Qatadah said: "That you may be questioned" means that you may be asked for something of your worldly goods, so that you may give to whom you wish and withhold from whom you wish, for you are people of wealth and blessing. They said this mockingly to them. Then Bukhtnassar pursued them, and the swords seized them. A caller cried out in the atmosphere of the sky: "O avengers of the prophets!" When they saw that, they confessed their sins, when it no longer benefited them.

﴿They said: "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾

﴿And that remained their cry﴾ — i.e., that phrase, which is their saying "Woe to us," was their supplication; they kept calling out with it and repeating it.

﴿until We made them as stubble﴾ — mowed down with the swords as grain is harvested, ﴿extinguished﴾ — dead.

His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ — i.e., in vain and without purpose.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 21, verses 17–20:**

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾. The scholars differed about the meaning of *al-lahw* (pastime). Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of 'Ata', said: "*al-lahw* is woman." This is also the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah. In the narration of al-Kalbi he said: "*al-lahw* is child," which is the view of al-Suddi. The first view is more apparent, because *al-wat'* (sexual intercourse) is called *lahw* in the Arabic language, and woman is the place of *al-wat'*. ﴿We would have taken it from Us﴾, meaning from Our presence, from the *hur al-'in* (wide-eyed maidens of paradise), not from you, the people of the earth. It was also said: the meaning is that if such a thing were permissible in His attributes, He would not take it in a way that appears to them; rather He would conceal it so that they would not perceive it.

The interpretation of the verse is that when the Christians said what they said about the Messiah and his mother, God refuted them with this and said: ﴿We would have taken it from Us﴾, because you know that a man's child and his wife remain with him, not with anyone else. ﴿If We were to do it﴾. Qatadah, Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj said: the *in* here is for negation, meaning: We were not doing it. It was also said: ﴿If We were to do it﴾ is conditional, meaning: if We were among those who do such a thing, We would have taken it from Us, but We did not do it, because it does not befit Lordship.

﴿Rather﴾, meaning: leave aside what they say, for it is falsehood and nonsense. ﴿We hurl﴾, meaning We throw down and impose, ﴿the truth﴾, meaning faith, ﴿upon falsehood﴾, meaning disbelief. It was also said: the truth is the word of God that He has no son, and the falsehood is their saying that God has taken a son. ﴿So it crushes it﴾, meaning destroys it. The root of *al-dam'* (crushing) is splitting the head until it reaches the brain. ﴿And behold, it vanishes﴾, meaning it departs. The meaning is: We nullify their lie by the truth We make clear, until it is annihilated and departs. Then He threatened them for their lying, saying: ﴿And woe to you﴾, O assembly of disbelievers, ﴿for what you describe﴾, meaning you describe God with what does not befit Him, such as a consort and a child. Mujahid said: "for what you lie about."

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, as servants and as dominion. ﴿And those near Him﴾, meaning the angels, ﴿are not too proud to worship Him﴾, meaning they do not disdain His worship and do not regard themselves as too great for it, ﴿nor do they tire﴾. It is said: *hasira* and *istahsara* mean one became weary and exhausted. Al-Suddi said: "they do not hold themselves too great to refrain from worship."

﴿They glorify Him night and day; they do not slacken﴾, meaning they do not grow weak and do not become bored. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "For them, glorifying God is like breathing is for the children of Adam."

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 21–24:**

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth?﴾ This is an interrogative (*istifham*) in the sense of denial. That is, they have not taken them. ﴿From the earth﴾ means idols made of wood and stone, and both are from the earth. ﴿Can they raise the dead?﴾ Divinity belongs only to the one who is able to give life, to create from non-existence, and to bestow the most eloquent forms of blessing.

﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah﴾ means, in the heavens and the earth, other than Allah, ﴿they would both have been ruined.﴾ That is, they would have been laid waste, and whoever is in them would have perished, because of the existence of mutual opposition among the gods. For every matter that proceeds from two or more is not conducted in order. Then He declared Himself free of imperfection, saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ That is, above what the polytheists attribute to Him of partners and offspring.

﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ and judges His creation, because He is the Lord, ﴿but they will be questioned﴾, that is, the creatures will be questioned about their actions and their deeds [[In "B": and their words.]] because they are servants. ﴿Or have they taken besides Him gods?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial and reproach. ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, that is, your argument for that. Then He said, beginning a new statement: ﴿This﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

﴿The reminder of those with me﴾: in it is the report about those with me in my religion and those who follow me until the Day of Resurrection, with what they have of reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience.

﴿And the reminder of those before me﴾ is a report about the earlier nations, what was done to them in this world and what will be done to them in the Hereafter. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, through the transmission of 'Ata': "The reminder of those with me" is the Qur'an, and "the reminder of those before me" is the Torah and the Gospel. Its meaning is: consult the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other books, and see whether you find in them that Allah has taken a son. ﴿But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.﴾

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 21–24:**

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth?﴾ This is an interrogative (*istifham*) in the sense of denial. That is, they have not taken them. ﴿From the earth﴾ means idols made of wood and stone, and both are from the earth. ﴿Can they raise the dead?﴾ Divinity belongs only to the one who is able to give life, to create from non-existence, and to bestow the most eloquent forms of blessing.

﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah﴾ means, in the heavens and the earth, other than Allah, ﴿they would both have been ruined.﴾ That is, they would have been laid waste, and whoever is in them would have perished, because of the existence of mutual opposition among the gods. For every matter that proceeds from two or more is not conducted in order. Then He declared Himself free of imperfection, saying: ﴿Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ That is, above what the polytheists attribute to Him of partners and offspring.

﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ and judges His creation, because He is the Lord, ﴿but they will be questioned﴾, that is, the creatures will be questioned about their actions and their deeds [[In "B": and their words.]] because they are servants. ﴿Or have they taken besides Him gods?﴾ This is an interrogative of denial and reproach. ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, that is, your argument for that. Then He said, beginning a new statement: ﴿This﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

﴿The reminder of those with me﴾: in it is the report about those with me in my religion and those who follow me until the Day of Resurrection, with what they have of reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience.

﴿And the reminder of those before me﴾ is a report about the earlier nations, what was done to them in this world and what will be done to them in the Hereafter. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, through the transmission of 'Ata': "The reminder of those with me" is the Qur'an, and "the reminder of those before me" is the Torah and the Gospel. Its meaning is: consult the Qur'an, the Torah, the Gospel, and all the other books, and see whether you find in them that Allah has taken a son. ﴿But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.﴾

﴿And We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him, saying: There is no god but I, so worship Me.﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *nuhi ilayhi* with a nun and a kasra on the ha, as an expression of glorification, in keeping with His words ﴿And We did not send﴾. The others read it with a ya and a fatha on the ha, as a passive verb. ﴿That there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾: affirm My unity.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son.﴾ It was revealed concerning Khuza'ah, when they said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾: He declared Himself free of what they said. ﴿Rather, they are servants﴾: that is, they are servants, meaning the angels, ﴿honored﴾. ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾: they do not go ahead of Him in speech, and they speak only what He commands them. ﴿And they act by His command﴾: its meaning is that they do not oppose Him in word or in deed.

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: that is, what they have done and what they are going to do. It was also said: what was before their creation and what will be after their creation. ﴿And they do not intercede except for one whom He approves﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, for whoever says: There is no god but Allah. Mujahid said: that is, for whomever He is pleased with. [[Al-Tabari mentioned both views: 17/16–17.]] ﴿And they are apprehensive out of fear of Him﴾: fearful, not feeling secure from His plotting.

﴿And whoever among them says: Indeed I am a god besides Him﴾. Qatadah said: it refers to Iblis, when he called to the worship of himself and commanded obedience to himself, for none of the angels ever said: I am a god besides Allah. ﴿That is how We will recompense him: Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, those who place divinity and worship in other than their rightful place.

Ibn Kathir recited "لم يَرَ" (lam yara, "did not see") without the waw [added from "b"], and it is written this way in their copies of the Qur'an (masahif). Its meaning is: "Did not those who disbelieved know" (alam ya'lam alladhina kafaru).

﴿Have not those who disbelieve seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We parted them?﴾ Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), 'Ata' and Qatadah said: they were one thing, joined together. ﴿And We parted them﴾ means We separated them by air. In the language (lughah), al-Ratq means closing up, and al-Fatq means splitting.

Ka'b said: Allah created the heavens and the earth lying upon one another. Then He created a wind, which entered between them [in "b": into their middle], and it split them apart.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: The heavens were closed up as one layer, and He split them and made them seven heavens. Likewise the earth was closed up as one layer, and He made it seven earths.

'Ikrimah and 'Atiyyah said: The sky was closed, not raining, and the earth was closed, not producing plants. So He split the sky with rain and the earth with plants. He said ﴿ratqan﴾ (closed) in the singular, though it describes the heavens and the earth, because it is a verbal noun (masdar) used in place of an adjective (ism), like al-Zawr (falsehood) and al-Sawm (fasting) and similar words.

﴿And We made﴾ [and We created] [omitted from "b"] ﴿from water every living thing﴾. That is: We gave life by the water that descends from the sky to every living thing, meaning animals. It also includes plants and trees. The meaning is that water is the cause of the life of everything. The commentators say [meaning] that every living thing is created from water, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah created every creature from water﴾ (Surah al-Nur: 45). Abu al-'Aliyah said: this means the sperm-drop (nutfah). If it is asked: Has Allah not created some living things from other than water? The answer: this is stated in terms of the majority, meaning that most living beings on earth are created from water or survive by water. ﴿Will they not then believe?﴾

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, that is, stable mountains, ﴿lest it shake with them﴾ [meaning: so that it would not shake with them]. [The words in brackets are omitted from "b".] ﴿And We made in them﴾, in the mountains, ﴿broad roads﴾, paths and passages. Al-Fajj is a wide road between two mountains. That is, We made roads between the mountains so that they might find their way to their destinations. ﴿Paths﴾ explains "broad roads". ﴿That perhaps they may be guided﴾.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 21, verses 32–33:**

﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾, from falling. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ (Al-Hajj: 65). It has also been said that it means protected from the devils by shooting stars. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And We guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ (Al-Hijr: 17). ﴿And they﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿from its signs﴾, meaning what God created in it of the sun, the moon, the stars and others, ﴿are turning away﴾, not reflecting on them and not taking warning from them.

﴿And it is He who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; each in an orbit (falak) they are swimming﴾. They run and move swiftly, like a swimmer in water. He said ﴿they are swimming﴾ and did not say "it is swimming," as is said of non-rational things, because He attributed to them the actions of rational beings, namely running and swimming, so they were referred to as rational beings.

The *falak* (orbit): it is the circuit of the stars that encloses them. In the speech of the Arabs, *falak* means anything that is round, its plural is *aflak*, and from it comes *falak al-mighzal* (the whorl of the spindle).

Al-Hasan said: The *falak* is a millstone, like the shape of the whorl of a spindle. He means that the course in which the stars run is round, like the rotation of a millstone.

Some of them said: The *falak* is the sky in which that star is located, so every star runs in the sky in which it was determined. This is the meaning of the saying of Qatadah.

Al-Kalbi said: The *falak* is the revolution of the sky.

Others said: The *falak* is a restrained wave beneath the sky in which the sun, the moon and the stars run.

[In manuscript B: al-Dahhak.]

[Al-Tabari mentioned some of these opinions and others, vol. 17, p. 23, then said: "The correct view on this matter is to say what God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿each in an orbit they are swimming﴾. It is possible that this orbit is as Mujahid said, like the iron of a millstone, and as was reported from al-Hasan, like the millstone of a mill. It is also possible that it is a restrained wave, or the pole of the sky. The reason is that *falak* in the speech of the Arabs is anything that revolves, its plural is *aflak*, and I have mentioned the saying of the rajaz poet:

*She spent the night conferring with the revolving falak.*

However, since whatever revolves is included in their speech, and there is no proof in the Book of God, nor in a report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), nor from one whose word is an authoritative excuse, indicating which of these it is, it is obligatory that we say what he said and remain silent about what we have no knowledge of. Since the correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is what we have mentioned, the interpretation of the statement is: ﴿and the sun and the moon, each in a revolving [orbit] they are swimming﴾."]

**The Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 21, verses 34–37:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, statement: ﴿And We did not grant to any human before you eternity﴾, meaning the lasting of remaining in this world. ﴿So if you die, will they be the ones who remain forever?﴾, meaning: will they remain forever if you die? This verse was revealed when they said, "We await for Muhammad the vicissitudes of time" (rayb al-manun).[[Mentioned by the author of Zad al-Masir: 5/350.]]

﴿Every soul will taste death. And We test you﴾, meaning We try you, ﴿with evil and with good﴾, meaning with hardship and ease, health and sickness, wealth and poverty. It is also said: with what you love and what you dislike. ﴿As a trial﴾, meaning a test, so that We may see how you will be grateful for what you love and patient with what you dislike. ﴿And to Us you will be returned.﴾

﴿And when those who disbelieve see you, they take you only as a mockery﴾ [meaning, they take you only] [[Omitted from manuscript "B".]] ﴿[only as a jest]﴾ [[Omitted from manuscript "B".]]. Al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. The Prophet ﷺ passed by him and he laughed and said, "This is the prophet of the Banu Abd Manaf."[[Al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/630 to Ibn Abi Hatim.]] ﴿Is this the one who﴾, meaning some of them say to others, "Is this the one who", ﴿mentions your gods﴾, meaning disparages them. It is said: "So-and-so mentions so-and-so," meaning he disparages him, and "So-and-so mentions Allah," meaning he magnifies and honors Him. ﴿While they are disbelievers in the mention of the Most Merciful.﴾ That is because they used to say, "We do not know the Most Merciful except Musaylimah." ﴿And they﴾: the second [pronoun] is a silah (a grammatical connective that completes the preceding phrase).

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, statement: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. The scholars differed about this. Some people said: its meaning is that his structure and creation are of haste, and he was molded upon it, as He said: ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾ (al-Isra' 17:11).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: When the soul entered the head and eyes of Adam, he looked at the fruits of Paradise. When it entered his body, he craved food, so he leapt, before the soul reached his feet, in haste toward the fruits of Paradise, and he fell. Thus it was said, "Man was created of haste." The intended meaning of "man" is Adam, and his offspring inherited haste. The Arabs say of one who does a thing excessively: "You were created from it," as they say: "You were created in play," and "You were created from anger," intending exaggeration in describing him with that. The statement of the Exalted confirms this: ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾.

Others said: its meaning is, "Man, meaning Adam, was created with haste in the creation of Allah for him," because his creation came after [the creation of] [[Addition from manuscript "B".]] everything at the end of the day on Friday, so He hastened in creating him before the sun set.

Mujahid said: When the soul gave life to his head, he said, "My Lord, hasten the creation of me before the sun sets." It is also said: [he was created] quickly and hastily, not following the ordinary sequence of the creation of the rest of the children of Adam from a drop of semen, a clinging clot, a lump of flesh, and so on.[[Al-Tabari cited these opinions: 17/26–27, then said: "The correct view in interpreting this, in our opinion, is that of those whom we mentioned who said its meaning is: man was created of haste in his creation, that is, with hurry and speed in that. This was said in this way because he was brought forward into creation before sunset in the last hour of the day of Friday, and at that time the soul was breathed into him. We have considered the sayings we mentioned to be most correct because of the statement of the Exalted: ‘I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten them’ as evidence for that. Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Amr informed us, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: ‘Indeed, on Friday there is an hour; no Muslim servant who asks Allah for good in it will coincide with it except that Allah gives it to him.’ Abd Allah ibn Salam said: I know which hour it is; it is the last hour of the day on Friday. It was said: "Nor from their backs the whips." ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ means they will be prevented from the punishment. The answer to "law" (lau, "if only") in His words ﴿If only those who disbelieved knew﴾ is omitted; its meaning is: "If they had known, they would not have persisted in their disbelief, nor would they have hastened, nor would they have said, 'When is this promise?'"

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 40–44:

﴿Nay, it will come upon them suddenly﴾, meaning the Hour, ﴿and will confound them﴾, that is, bewilder them. It is said: "So-and-so is mabhut," meaning bewildered. ﴿So they will not be able to avert it, nor will they be given respite﴾, meaning they will not be granted delay.

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who mocked them were engulfed﴾ by what they used to mock, meaning: the recompense of their mockery descended upon them. ﴿That which they used to mock at﴾ is what they used to mock.

﴿Say: Who protects you﴾, that is, guards you, ﴿by night and day from the Most Merciful?﴾ If He sends His punishment upon you. Ibn 'Abbas said: who will prevent you from the punishment of the Most Merciful? ﴿Nay, they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, meaning from the Qur'an and the admonitions of Allah, ﴿refusing﴾. ﴿Or do they have gods that defend them against Us?﴾ Here "am" (أم) is extra in this and similar usages. There is inversion in the verse; its sense is: "Or do they have gods, other than Us, that defend them?" Then He described the gods as weak, saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are unable to help themselves﴾, that is, to protect themselves, so how could they help their worshippers? ﴿Nor can they be protected from Us﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be prevented. 'Ata' said: they will be given protection from Him; the Arabs say: "I am your protector (jar) and companion (sahib) against so-and-so," meaning I grant protection from him. Mujahid said: they will be helped. Qatadah said: they will not be granted good from Allah.

﴿Nay, We gave these people﴾, the disbelievers, ﴿and their fathers﴾ enjoyment in this world, that is, We granted them respite. It was also said: We gave them blessings, ﴿until the life span grew long for them﴾, that is, time extended for them, so they became deluded.

﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its extremities?﴾ Meaning: what We diminish from the extremities of the polytheists and add to the extremities of the believers, referring to the rise of the Prophet ﷺ and his conquest of the abodes of polytheism, land by land. ﴿Are they then the victors, or are We?﴾

﴿Nay, it will come upon them suddenly﴾, meaning the Hour, ﴿and will confound them﴾, that is, bewilder them. It is said: "So-and-so is mabhut," meaning bewildered. ﴿So they will not be able to avert it, nor will they be given respite﴾, meaning they will not be granted delay.

﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who mocked them were engulfed﴾ by what they used to mock, meaning: the recompense of their mockery descended upon them. ﴿That which they used to mock at﴾ is what they used to mock.

﴿Say: Who protects you﴾, that is, guards you, ﴿by night and day from the Most Merciful?﴾ If He sends His punishment upon you. Ibn 'Abbas said: who will prevent you from the punishment of the Most Merciful? ﴿Nay, they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾, meaning from the Qur'an and the admonitions of Allah, ﴿refusing﴾. ﴿Or do they have gods that defend them against Us?﴾ Here "am" (أم) is extra in this and similar usages. There is inversion in the verse; its sense is: "Or do they have gods, other than Us, that defend them?" Then He described the gods as weak, saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are unable to help themselves﴾, that is, to protect themselves, so how could they help their worshippers? ﴿Nor can they be protected from Us﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they will be prevented. 'Ata' said: they will be given protection from Him; the Arabs say: "I am your protector (jar) and companion (sahib) against so-and-so," meaning I grant protection from him. Mujahid said: they will be helped. Qatadah said: they will not be granted good from Allah.

﴿Nay, We gave these people﴾, the disbelievers, ﴿and their fathers﴾ enjoyment in this world, that is, We granted them respite. It was also said: We gave them blessings, ﴿until the life span grew long for them﴾, that is, time extended for them, so they became deluded.

﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its extremities?﴾ Meaning: what We diminish from the extremities of the polytheists and add to the extremities of the believers, referring to the rise of the Prophet ﷺ and his conquest of the abodes of polytheism, land by land. ﴿Are they then the victors, or are We?﴾

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 45–47:**

﴿Say: I only warn you by the revelation.﴾ That is, I warn you with the Qur'an. ﴿But the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned.﴾ Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿tusma'u﴾ (*tusma'u*, "you cause to hear") with a *ta'* and a *damma* on it, and with a *kasra* on the *mim*, and ﴿al-summu﴾ (*al-summu*, "the deaf") in the accusative (*nusiba*). He made the address directed to the Prophet (ﷺ). The others recited it with a *ya'* and a *fatha* on it, and with a *fatha* on the *mim*, and ﴿al-summu﴾ in the nominative (*rufi'a*). ﴿When they are warned﴾ means when they are made afraid.

﴿And if a breath of your Lord's punishment touches them﴾ means if it reaches them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "a portion." It was also said: "a little." Ibn Jurayj said: "a share," from the expression "so-and-so *nafaha* (gave a share) from his wealth to so-and-so," meaning he gave him a portion of it. It was also said: "a strike," from the expression "the animal *nafahat* with its leg," when it kicks. ﴿They will surely say: O woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers.﴾ That is, by our destruction, indeed we were polytheists. They called down woe upon themselves after they had acknowledged polytheism.

﴿And We will set up the scales of justice﴾ means scales possessing justice, and *al-qist* means justice. ﴿For the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything.﴾ Nothing will be diminished from the reward of its good deeds, nor will anything be added to its evil deeds. In the reports it is related: "Indeed the scale has a tongue and two pans."[[Al-Lalika'i related it in *Sharh Usul I'tiqad Ahl al-Sunnah*, 6/1173, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman, who said: "The scale was mentioned in the presence of al-Hasan, and he said: It has a tongue and two pans." Many hadiths support this. See: *Sharh al-Tahawiyyah*, pp. 480–484; *Lawami' al-Anwar al-Bahiyyah* by al-Saffarini, 2/184–186.]]

It is related that Dawud, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to show him the scale. He was shown each pan as wide as what lies between the east and the west, and he fainted. Then he regained consciousness and said: "O my God, who can fill its pan with good deeds?" He said: "O Dawud, indeed when I am pleased with My servant, I fill it with a date."[[Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in *al-Tadhkirah*; see *Lawami' al-Anwar al-Bahiyyah*, 2/184.]]

﴿And if it is the weight of a grain of mustard seed﴾: the people of Madina recited ﴿mithqal﴾ (*mithqalu*, "weight") with a *raf'* (nominative) on the *lam* here and in Surat Luqman, meaning "if the weight of a grain should occur." The others put it in the accusative (*nasaba*), on the meaning: "if that thing is the weight of a grain," that is, equal in weight to a grain of mustard seed. ﴿We will bring it﴾ means We will produce it, so that We may recompense with it.

﴿And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾. Al-Suddi said: "as counters," and *al-hasb* means counting. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "knowing and preserving," because whoever counts something knows it and preserves it.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the Furqan (the criterion, that which distinguishes truth from falsehood)﴾. He means the Book that separates truth from falsehood, which is the Tawrah (Torah).

Ibn Zayd said: al-Furqan means victory over the enemies, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not send down upon Our servant on the day of al-Furqan﴾ (al-Anfal: 41), meaning the day of Badr, because He said ﴿and a light (diya')﴾. He introduced the waw (the conjunction "and") there, meaning: We gave Moses the victory and the light, which is the Tawrah.

Whoever says that al-Furqan refers to the Tawrah says: the waw in His words ﴿and a light﴾ is extra and superfluous, meaning: We gave him the Tawrah as a light. It was also said: it is another attribute of the Tawrah. ﴿And a reminder (dhikr)﴾, meaning a reminder, ﴿for those who are mindful of Allah﴾, ﴿who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾, meaning they fear Him though they have not seen Him, ﴿and who dread the Hour﴾, meaning they are fearful.

﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾, meaning the Qur'an. It is a reminder for whoever takes heed through it, and blessed, meaning one seeks blessing through it and seeks good from it. ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾, O people of Makkah, ﴿deny it?﴾ (i.e., reject it). This is a question of rebuke and reproach.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And We indeed gave Ibrahim his rushd (right guidance) before this﴾. Al-Qurtubi said: meaning his righteousness. ﴿Before this﴾, meaning before Moses and Aaron. The exegetes said: his rushd, meaning his guidance, ﴿before this﴾, meaning before puberty, which is when he came out of the cave while he was young. He means: We guided him while he was young, as the Exalted said concerning Yahya, peace be upon him: ﴿And We gave him wisdom while he was a child﴾ (Maryam: 12). ﴿And We knew him well﴾, that he was worthy of guidance and prophethood.

﴿"And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾, I will scheme against them, ﴿after you have turned your backs and gone away."﴾ That is, after you have turned away, departing for your festival.

Mujahid and Qatadah said: Ibrahim only said this in secret from his people, and no one heard it except one man, who then disclosed it about him, saying: "We heard a youth mentioning them, called Ibrahim."

Al-Suddi said: They had a gathering and a festival every year, and when they returned from their festival they would enter upon the idols and prostrate to them, then return to their homes. When that festival came, Ibrahim's father said to him: "O Ibrahim, if you came out with us to our festival, our religion would please you." So Ibrahim went out with them. When they reached part of the way, he threw himself down and said, "Indeed, I am sick," meaning, "I am complaining of my foot." When they had gone on, he called out after them, while only the weak among the people had remained: ﴿"And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols"﴾, and they heard him say it. Then Ibrahim returned to the house of the gods. They were in a great hall, and facing the entrance of the hall was a great idol, and beside it was a smaller one, and the idols were placed beside one another, each idol next to one smaller than it, up to the door of the hall. They had set out food and placed it before the gods, saying, "When we return, and the gods have blessed our food, we will eat." When Ibrahim looked at them and at the food before them, he said to them, mockingly, "Will you not eat?" When they did not answer him, he said, "What is wrong with you that you do not speak?" Then he turned upon them, striking with his right hand, and began breaking them in pieces, until only the largest idol remained. He hung the axe around its neck and then went out. ﴿That is what His words, mighty and majestic, refer to.﴾ [Narrated by al-Tabari, 17/38; see al-Durr al-Manthur, 5/636–637.]

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 58–61:

﴿So he made them into fragments﴾. Al-Kisa'i (a Qur'anic reader) read *jidadan* (جِذَاذًا) with a kasra on the jim, meaning broken pieces and fragments, the plural of *jadhidh* (جَذِيذ), which is dry crumbled material, like *khafif* and *khifaf*. The others read it with a damma, like *hutam* and *rufat* (both meaning debris). ﴿except a large one among them﴾, for he did not break it, and he placed the axe on its neck. It was said that he tied the axe to its hand. There were seventy-two idols: some were of gold, some of silver, some of iron, lead, tin, wood, and stone. The large idol was of gold, adorned with jewels, and in its eyes were two rubies that glittered. God's words: ﴿that perhaps they may return to it﴾. It was said: the meaning is that perhaps they would return to his religion and to what he calls them to, when they knew the weakness and helplessness of the gods. It was also said: perhaps they would return to him and ask him. When the people returned from their festival to the house of their gods and saw their idols in fragments.

﴿They said: Who has done this to our gods? Indeed he is among the wrongdoers﴾, that is, among the criminals.

﴿They said﴾, meaning those who heard Abraham's words: ﴿And by God, I will surely scheme against your idols﴾. ﴿We heard a youth mention them﴾, meaning disparaging and reviling them, ﴿called Abraham﴾. It is he whom we suspect did this. So the news reached Nimrod the tyrant and the nobles of his people.

﴿They said: Then bring him before the eyes of the people﴾. Nimrod said: that is, bring him out openly, in the sight of the people, ﴿that they may bear witness﴾ against him that he is the one who did it. They disliked seizing him without proof. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: ﴿that they may bear witness﴾ means that they may attend his punishment and what is done to him.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 62–64:

﴿They said﴾ to him: ﴿"Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾

﴿He said﴾, Ibrahim: ﴿"Rather, this one, their chief, did it. So ask them, if they can speak."﴾ He was angered that they worshipped these small ones alongside him while he was greater than them, so he broke them. Ibrahim intended by this to establish the proof against them, and this is the meaning of his saying: ﴿"So ask them, if they can speak"﴾, so that they would be told who did this to them.

Al-Qutaybi said: The meaning is "Rather, their chief did it, if they can speak," as a conditional. He made speech a condition for the act, meaning: if they are able to speak, they are able to act. Thus he showed them their inability to speak, and implicit within it [[In "b" its pronoun.]] is "I did it."

It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that he used to pause at his saying ﴿"Rather, this one did it"﴾ and would say: its meaning is that [[Addition from "b".]] whoever did it. The first interpretation is more correct, because of what is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ibrahim did not lie except three lies, two of them concerning the sake of Allah: his saying ﴿"Indeed, I am sick"﴾ (al-Saffat: 89), and his saying ﴿"Rather, this one, their chief, did it"﴾, and his saying to Sarah ﴿"This is my sister"﴾." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Anbiya', chapter on the saying of Allah Most High: "And Allah took Ibrahim as a friend," 6/388, and by Muslim in al-Fada'il, chapter on the virtues of Ibrahim the Friend (ﷺ), no. (2371), 4/1840.]] It was said regarding his saying ﴿"Indeed, I am sick"﴾ that it means "I will become sick," and it was said: "sickness of the heart," meaning he was grieved over your misguidance. As for his saying to Sarah, "This is my sister," it means in religion. These interpretations are to negate lying from Ibrahim, but the first is preferable because of the hadith concerning it. It is possible that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, permitted him to do so for the purpose of good and of rebuking them and establishing the proof against them, just as He permitted Yusuf, when [[In "b" when.]] he commanded his caller to say to his brothers: ﴿"O caravan, you are indeed thieves"﴾ (Yusuf: 70). And they had not stolen.

﴿So they returned to themselves﴾, meaning they reflected with their hearts and returned to their intellects, ﴿and said﴾: "We see that he is only as he said: ﴿'Indeed, you are the wrongdoers'﴾", meaning by worshipping what does not speak. It was also said: "You are the wrongdoers" toward this man in your questioning him, while these gods of yours are present, so ask them.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 21, verses 65–68:**

﴿Then they were turned back upon their heads.﴾ The people of tafsir (exegesis) said: Allah caused the truth to flow upon their tongues in their first statement, then wretchedness overtook them. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Then they were turned back upon their heads﴾, meaning they were returned to disbelief after they had acknowledged themselves to be wrongdoers. Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 69:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had He not said 'safety,' Abraham would have died from its coldness. It is well known in the reports that on that day no fire remained on earth except that it was extinguished, so no one in the world benefited from fire that day. And had He not said 'and safety upon Abraham,' it would have remained cold forever." [[The author of Adwa' al-Bayan mentioned these statements: 4 / 589.]]

As-Suddi said: "The angels took hold of Abraham by his arms and seated him on the ground, and there was a spring of sweet water, red roses and narcissus." [[See: Zad al-Masir: 5 / 367.]]

Ka'b said: "The fire burned nothing of Abraham except his bonds." [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 17 / 44.]] They said: "Abraham remained in that place for seven days." [[See: Zad al-Masir: 5 / 367; al-Qurtubi: 11 / 304.]]

Al-Minhal ibn 'Amr said: Abraham said, "I never had days more pleasant than the days I spent in the fire." [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 17 / 44, and Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir: 4 / 185.]]

Ibn Yasar said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent the angel of shade in the form of Abraham, and he sat beside Abraham in the fire to keep him company." They said: "Allah sent Gabriel with a shirt from the silk of Paradise and a carpet, and he clothed him in the shirt and seated him on the carpet, and sat with him conversing with him. Gabriel said, 'O Abraham, your Lord says: Do you not know that the fire does not harm My beloved ones?'" [[See Zad al-Masir: 5 / 367.]]

Then Nimrod looked out and gazed upon Abraham from a lofty palace he had, and saw him sitting in a garden with the angel seated beside him, and around him was fire burning the firewood. He called out to him: "O Abraham, great is your God, whose power has reached the point that it prevented you from what I see. O Abraham, are you able to come out of it?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Do you fear that if you remain in it, it will harm you?" He said, "No." He said, "Then rise and come out of it." Abraham rose and walked in it until he came out of it. When he came out to him, he said to him: "O Abraham, who is the man I saw with you in your form, sitting beside you?" He said, "That is the angel of shade, whom my Lord sent to me to keep me company in it." Nimrod said: "O Abraham, I will offer a sacrifice to your God because of what I have seen of His power and might in what He did for you, when you refused anything but worshipping Him and affirming His oneness. I will slaughter for Him four thousand cows." Abraham said to him: "In that case, God will not accept from you what you have been upon of your religion until you leave it for my religion." He said: "I cannot give up my kingdom. But I will slaughter them for Him." So Nimrod slaughtered them for Him, then ceased from Abraham, and God protected him from him. Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 72–73:

﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as a additional gift (nafilah)﴾ Mujahid and Ata' said: the meaning of nafilah is a gift; both of them are from Allah's gift, a nafilah, meaning a gift. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: an extra favour. And it is narrated from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Zayd and Qatadah, may Allah be pleased with them: the nafilah is Jacob, because Allah, mighty and majestic, granted him Isaac in answer to his prayer when he said: ﴿Grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ (al-Saffat: 100). And Jacob was an addition [walad al-walad]. [[In "B": a child to his child.]] And nafilah means an increase, ﴿And We made them all righteous﴾, meaning: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

﴿And We made them leaders﴾ who are followed in goodness, ﴿guiding by Our command﴾ calling people to Our religion, ﴿and We inspired in them the doing of good deeds﴾ acting according to the laws (shara'i'), ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾ meaning: observing it diligently, ﴿and the giving of zakah﴾ paying it [[Addition from "B".]] ﴿and they were worshippers of Us﴾ monotheists.

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 74–78:**

﴿And Lot, We gave him﴾, i.e., "And We gave Lot," and it was said: "Remember Lot, to whom We gave" ﴿judgment﴾, meaning the decisive judgment between disputants in truth, ﴿and knowledge﴾. ﴿And We delivered him from the town that used to commit abominations﴾, meaning Sodom. Its people used to have intercourse with males in their backsides and would break wind in their assemblies, along with other reprehensible deeds that they committed. ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient﴾. ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy. Indeed, he was among the righteous﴾.

﴿And Noah, when he called out﴾, i.e., supplicated, ﴿before﴾, meaning before Abraham and Lot. ﴿So We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: from the drowning and from the denial of his people. It was also said: because he was the longest-lived of the prophets and the most afflicted by trials. And al-Karb (distress) means extreme grief [[Omitted from "ب".]].

﴿And We supported him﴾, i.e., We protected him, ﴿against the people who denied Our signs﴾, so that they could not reach him with harm. Abu 'Ubaydah said: meaning "against the people." ﴿Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all﴾.

The statement of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field﴾. The scholars differed concerning al-Harth (the field). Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, and most of the exegetes said: the field was a vineyard whose clusters were hanging. Qatadah said: it was a sown field. ﴿When the sheep of a people grazed in it﴾, i.e., they pastured in it at night and ruined it. Al-Nafsh is grazing at night, while al-Hamal is grazing by day, and both mean grazing without a shepherd. ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾, i.e., this occurred with Our knowledge and in Our sight, and its knowledge was not hidden from Us. Al-Farra' said: He used the plural for two, saying "li-hukmihim" (their judgment), while he meant David and Solomon, because two is a plural. This is like His statement: ﴿But if he has brothers, then for his mother is a sixth﴾ (al-Nisa': 11), while he meant two brothers.

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and al-Zuhri said: That is because two men entered upon David, one of them the owner of a field and the other the owner of sheep. The owner of the crop said: "This man's sheep got loose at night and fell into my field and ruined it, so nothing remained of it." David gave him the sheep in exchange for the field. The two went out and passed by Solomon, who said: "How did he judge between you?" They informed him, and Solomon said: "If I were in charge of their affair, I would have judged other than this."

It is narrated that he said: "Other than this is gentler to both parties." David was informed of that, so he summoned him and said: "How would you judge?" It is also narrated that he said: "By the right of prophethood and fatherhood, will you not inform me of what is gentler to both parties?" He said: "Give the sheep to the owner of the field, so he benefits from their milk, offspring, wool and other benefits, and the owner of the sheep sows for the owner of the field a field like his field. When the field returns to the condition it was in on the day it was consumed, it is delivered to its people, and the owner of the sheep takes his sheep." David said: "The judgment is what you have judged," and he ruled accordingly [[Al-Tabari narrated these two reports: 17/51–54. See also Ibn Kathir's Tafsir: 3/187.]].

It was said: when Solomon judged, he was eleven years old. As for the ruling of Islam [in this matter] [[Addition from "ب".]]: whatever livestock left to roam by day destroys the property of another, its owner bears no liability for it; whatever it destroys at night, its owner is liable for it, because it is the custom of people that owners of crops guard them by day, while livestock graze by day and are returned to the pen at night.

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us, Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us, Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us, Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Abu Shihab, from Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisah, that a she-camel belonging to al-Bara' ibn 'Azib entered an orchard and ruined it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that it is incumbent upon the owners of orchards to guard them by day, and that whatever livestock destroys at night is the liability of its owners. The proponents of opinion (ra'y, personal reasoning) held that if the owner is not with his animals, he is not liable for what his livestock destroys, whether by night or by day [[Abu Dawud narrated it in al-Buyu', chapter: "Livestock destroying the crops of a people," 5/202. Al-Mundhiri attributed it to al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra and to Ibn Majah in al-Ahkam, chapter: "The ruling on what livestock destroys," no. 2333, 2/781. Malik narrated it in al-Muwatta' as mursal (with a missing companion in the chain): 2/747–748. Also narrated by Ahmad: 4/295; 'Abd al-Razzaq: 10/82; and al-Bayhaqi: 8/341–342. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in al-Tamhid (11/81–82): "As far as I know, all the transmitters of al-Muwatta' narrated it as mursal, and likewise the students of Ibn Shihab narrated it from him as mursal, except that Ibn 'Uyaynah narrated it from al-Zuhri from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Haram ibn Sa'd ibn Muhayyisah..." He then said: "This hadith, although mursal, is a well-known hadith; the imams transmitted it as mursal, the trustworthy narrators related it, the jurists of the Hijaz acted upon it and accepted it, and it was practiced in Medina. Al-Shafi'i claimed that he examined the mursal reports of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and found them sound, and most jurists rely upon them." Ibn al-Turkumani said in al-Jawhar al-Naqi (8/342): "The chain of this hadith is severely disordered, and it was narrated from al-Zuhri in seven different ways, mentioned by Ibn al-Qattan."]].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾, meaning: We taught him the judgment and inspired it to Solomon. ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾, meaning Dawud and Sulayman. Al-Hasan said: "Were it not for this verse, I would have seen the judges destroyed. But God praised this one for his correctness and commended that one for his effort (ijtihad)" [[See: al-Qurtubi: 11 / 309.]]. The scholars differed over whether the judgment of Dawud was by ijtihad (independent reasoning) or by explicit text, and likewise the judgment of Sulayman.

Some of them said: it was by ijtihad. They said: ijtihad is permissible for the prophets, so that they may attain the reward of the mujtahids, except that Dawud erred and Sulayman was correct. They said: error is permissible for the prophets, except that they are not left to persist in it. As for the scholars, they have the right of ijtihad in new matters when they find no explicit text in the Book or the Sunnah, and if they err, there is no sin upon them [[For a detailed discussion see al-Qurtubi: 11 / 308 - 310, and Adwa' al-Bayan 4 / 596 - 597, where Shaykh al-Shinqiti - may God have mercy on him - preferred that their judgment, that of Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them), was by ijtihad and not by revelation, as he says: "In the verse there are two indications that their judgment was by ijtihad and not by revelation: that Sulayman was correct and deserved praise for his ijtihad and his correctness, and that Dawud did not hit the mark, yet he deserved praise for his ijtihad and was not subject to blame or censure for not being correct, just as He praised Sulayman for correctness in His saying: (So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman), and praised both of them in His saying: (And to each We gave judgment and knowledge). His saying (when they both judged) shows that they both judged in the case, each with a judgment differing from the other's; had it been revelation, the disagreement would not have been permissible. Then He said: (So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman), which shows that Dawud was not given understanding of it; had his judgment in it been by revelation, he would have been given understanding of it, as you see. So His saying (when they both judged) together with His saying (So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman) is an indication that the judgment was not by revelation but by ijtihad, and Sulayman was correct in it while Dawud was not, by God's granting him that understanding. The second indication is that His saying, exalted is He: (So We gave understanding of it...), the verse, shows that He gave him understanding of it from the texts of the law they already had, not that He sent down to him a new revelation abrogating it, for His saying (So We gave understanding of it) is more fitting to the first than to the second, as you see."]].

[It is lifted from them] [[Addition from manuscript "b".]] because of what was narrated to us by Abd al-Wahhab ibn Muhammad al-Khatib, who said: Abd al-Aziz ibn Ahmad al-Khallal informed us, who said: Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm informed us, who said: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman informed us, who said: al-Shafi'i informed us, who said: Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad informed us, from Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Hadi, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi, from Bishr ibn Sa'id, from Abu [...] from Qays, client of Amr ibn al-As, from Amr ibn al-As, that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "When a judge judges and exerts himself (ijtihad) and is correct, he has two rewards; and when he judges and exerts himself and errs, he has one reward" [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-I'tisam, chapter: The reward of the judge when he exerts himself and is correct or errs: 13 / 318; and Muslim in al-Aqdiyah, chapter: The reward of the judge when he exerts himself and is correct or errs, no. (1716), 3 / 1342; and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 10 / 115.]].

And a people said: Dawud and Sulayman judged by revelation, and the judgment of Sulayman abrogated the judgment of Dawud. This speaker says: it is not permissible for the prophets to judge by ijtihad, because they are independent of ijtihad through revelation. They also said: error is not permissible for the prophets [[See al-Qurtubi: 11 / 308 - 310.]]. Those who held that every mujtahid is correct argued from the apparent meaning of the verse and from the report, in that it promises reward to the mujtahid even in error; this is the view of the proponents of opinion (ahl al-ra'y). A group held that not every mujtahid is correct; rather, when the ijtihad of mujtahids differs on a case, the truth lies with one of them without specification, and if each were correct, the division would have no meaning. As for his peace be upon him saying: "and when he exerts himself and errs, he has a reward," it does not mean that he is rewarded for the error, but that he is rewarded for his exertion in seeking the truth, since his ijtihad is an act of worship, and the sin of error is lifted from him when he has spared no effort [[See al-Qurtubi: 11 / 311.]].

Abu al-Wahid al-Malihi informed us, who said: Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, who said: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, who said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, who said: Abu al-Yaman informed us, who said: Shu'ayb informed us, from al-Zuhri, who said: Abu al-Zinad informed us, from Abd al-Rahman al-A'raj, that he heard Abu Hurayrah that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Two women were with their two sons, when a wolf came and took away the son of one of them. The other woman said: 'It was your son that he took.' The first said: 'It was your son that he took.' So they brought their dispute to Dawud, who judged it for the elder. Then they went out to Sulayman and informed him, and he said: 'Bring me a knife, that I may split him between them.' The younger said: 'Do not do that, may God have mercy on you; he is her son.' So he judged it for the younger" [[Related by al-Bukhari in al-Anbiya', chapter: the saying of God, the Exalted: (And to Dawud We gave Sulayman; an excellent servant, indeed he was ever turning back in repentance): 6 / 458; and Muslim in al-Aqdiyah, chapter: the explanation of the disagreement of mujtahids, no. (1720), 3 / 1343.]].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] with Dawud, and the birds﴾, meaning: We subjected the mountains and the birds to glorify [God] along with Dawud when he glorified [God]. Ibn Abbas said: he understood the glorification of stones and trees. Wahb said: the mountains would respond to him with glorification, and likewise the birds. Qatadah said: "they glorify" means they pray along with him when he prays. It was also said: when Dawud grew slack, God would make him hear the glorification of the mountains and birds, so that he would be energized in glorifying and yearn for it.

﴿And We were doers﴾

Meaning: of what has been mentioned, the granting of understanding, the giving of judgment, and the subjecting [of creation].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 80–81:

﴿And We taught him the making of armor for you﴾. The word *al-libus* (armor) here means *al-duruʿ* (coats of mail), because they are worn (*tulbas*). In the lexicon (*lughah*), *libus* is a name for everything that is worn, and it is used for all weapons. It means *al-malbus* (that which is worn), like *al-julus* (sitting) and *al-rukub* (riding). Qatadah said: "The first to make coats of mail, to link them and to ring them was Dawud. Before that they were plates." The coat of mail combines lightness and protection. ﴿To protect you﴾ means to guard you and shield you. ﴿From your violence﴾ means from the war of your enemy. al-Suddi said: "From the impact of weapons upon you."

Abu Ja'far, Ibn ʿAmir, Hafs from ʿAsim, and Ya'qub read ﴿*li-tuhsinakum*﴾ with the *ta'* (feminine), meaning the craft (*al-sanʿah*). Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read it with the *nun* (*nun*), in accordance with His saying ﴿And We taught him﴾. The others read it with the *ya'* (masculine), making the verb refer to the armor (*al-libus*). It was also said: the meaning is "that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may protect you." ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ This is addressed to Dawud and his family. It was also said: it is addressed to the people of Makkah, meaning "Will you then be grateful for My blessings by obeying the Messenger?"

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind, violent⁠﴾. That is, We subjected the wind to Sulayman. The wind is moving air, a subtle body which, because of its subtlety, cannot be grasped, and which becomes evident to the senses through its movement. *al-rih* may be masculine or feminine. ﴿Violent﴾ means very strong in its blowing. If it is asked: He said elsewhere ﴿flowing gently by his command﴾, and *rukhaʾ* means gentle? It is answered: the wind was under his command. If he wished it to be strong, it became strong, and if he wished it to be gentle, it became gentle. ﴿It flowed by his command to the land which We had blessed﴾, meaning al-Sham (Syria). That is because it flowed for Sulayman and his companions wherever Sulayman wished, then returned to his dwelling in al-Sham. ﴿And We were of all things⁠﴾ that We taught him, ﴿knowing﴾ the soundness of the management in it. We knew that what was given to Sulayman, of the subjugation of the wind and other things, would lead him to submit to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When Sulayman, peace be upon him, went out to his assembly, the birds gathered around him, and the jinn and humans stood for him until he sat on his throne. He was a warrior king who rarely stayed back from campaign. No king in any region of the earth was heard of without his coming to him until he humbled him. It is claimed that when he wished to campaign, he ordered his camp to be set up, and it was pitched on wooden platforms. Then he loaded upon it the people, the animals, and the instruments of war. When he had loaded what he wished, he commanded the violent wind, and it came beneath that wooden platform and lifted it, until once it had risen with him, he commanded the gentle wind, and it carried him for a month in its evening journey and a month in its morning journey to wherever he wished. The gentle wind would pass over his army and over the field without stirring it, without raising dust, and without harming a bird. Wahb said: "It was related to me that at a dwelling by the bank of the Tigris, written in it [*kataba-hu*] [[omitted in manuscript A]] by one of Sulayman's companions, whether from the jinn or from humans: 'We alighted here, and we did not build what we found built. We set out in the morning from Istakhr, and we halted here, and we will set out from it, if Allah wills, and spend the night in al-Sham.'"

Muqatil said: The devils wove for Sulayman a carpet one farsakh by one farsakh, of gold woven into silk. A golden pulpit was set for him in the middle of the carpet, and he sat upon it. Around him were three thousand chairs of gold and silver. The prophets sat on the golden chairs and the scholars on the silver chairs, and around them were the people, and around the people were the jinn and the devils. The birds shaded him with their wings so that the sun did not touch him. The east wind lifted the carpet a distance of a month, from morning to afternoon and from afternoon to morning.

And on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Six hundred thousand chairs would be set out for Sulayman. The humans would sit nearest to him, then the jinn after them, then the birds would shade them, and then the wind would carry them.

al-Hasan said: When horses occupied the Prophet of Allah Sulayman, peace be upon him, until the afternoon prayer (*salat al-ʿasr*) passed him by, he became angry for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and he slaughtered the horses. Allah replaced them for him with something better than them. The fastest of the winds flowed by his command as he wished. He would set out in the morning from Iliya, take his midday rest at Istakhr, and then depart from it in the evening, so that his evening arrival would be at Babil.

Ibn Zayd said: He had a vessel of wood, and in it were a thousand corners, and in each corner a thousand chambers. The humans and jinn rode with him in it, and beneath each corner were a thousand devils who lifted that vessel. When it rose, the gentle wind came and carried it along with them. He would take his midday rest with a people between him and whom was a month's distance, and he would be in the evening with a people between him and whom was a month's distance. The people did not know until the armies had come upon them with him.

It is related that Sulayman journeyed from the land of Iraq in the morning and reached the city of Marw, and he prayed the afternoon prayer in the city of Balkh. The wind carried him and his armies, and the birds shaded them. Then he traveled from the city of Balkh, passing through the lands of the Turks, and then came to the lands of China, covering in the morning a distance of a month and in the afternoon the same. Then he turned to the right, away from the rising of the sun, along the shore of the sea, until he reached the land of Qandahar. He went out from it to the land of Makran and Kirman, then passed beyond them until he reached the land of Fars. He stayed there for days, set out from it in the morning, and halted at Kaskar. Then he departed for al-Sham, and his place of settlement was the city of Tadmur. Before his departure from al-Sham to Iraq, he had commanded the devils, and they built it for him with marble slabs, pillars, and white and yellow marble. The Nabigha said regarding this:

*Except Sulayman, when the King said to him:*
*"Rise up in the wilderness and mark out its boundaries [for the jinn]..."*

*And I have permitted the host of jinn*
*to build Tadmur with slabs and pillars.*

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 80–81:

﴿And We taught him the making of armor for you﴾. The word *al-libus* (armor) here means *al-duruʿ* (coats of mail), because they are worn (*tulbas*). In the lexicon (*lughah*), *libus* is a name for everything that is worn, and it is used for all weapons. It means *al-malbus* (that which is worn), like *al-julus* (sitting) and *al-rukub* (riding). Qatadah said: "The first to make coats of mail, to link them and to ring them was Dawud. Before that they were plates." The coat of mail combines lightness and protection. ﴿To protect you﴾ means to guard you and shield you. ﴿From your violence﴾ means from the war of your enemy. al-Suddi said: "From the impact of weapons upon you."

Abu Ja'far, Ibn ʿAmir, Hafs from ʿAsim, and Ya'qub read ﴿*li-tuhsinakum*﴾ with the *ta'* (feminine), meaning the craft (*al-sanʿah*). Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read it with the *nun* (*nun*), in accordance with His saying ﴿And We taught him﴾. The others read it with the *ya'* (masculine), making the verb refer to the armor (*al-libus*). It was also said: the meaning is "that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may protect you." ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ This is addressed to Dawud and his family. It was also said: it is addressed to the people of Makkah, meaning "Will you then be grateful for My blessings by obeying the Messenger?"

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And to Sulayman [We subjected] the wind, violent⁠﴾. That is, We subjected the wind to Sulayman. The wind is moving air, a subtle body which, because of its subtlety, cannot be grasped, and which becomes evident to the senses through its movement. *al-rih* may be masculine or feminine. ﴿Violent﴾ means very strong in its blowing. If it is asked: He said elsewhere ﴿flowing gently by his command﴾, and *rukhaʾ* means gentle? It is answered: the wind was under his command. If he wished it to be strong, it became strong, and if he wished it to be gentle, it became gentle. ﴿It flowed by his command to the land which We had blessed﴾, meaning al-Sham (Syria). That is because it flowed for Sulayman and his companions wherever Sulayman wished, then returned to his dwelling in al-Sham. ﴿And We were of all things⁠﴾ that We taught him, ﴿knowing﴾ the soundness of the management in it. We knew that what was given to Sulayman, of the subjugation of the wind and other things, would lead him to submit to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When Sulayman, peace be upon him, went out to his assembly, the birds gathered around him, and the jinn and humans stood for him until he sat on his throne. He was a warrior king who rarely stayed back from campaign. No king in any region of the earth was heard of without his coming to him until he humbled him. It is claimed that when he wished to campaign, he ordered his camp to be set up, and it was pitched on wooden platforms. Then he loaded upon it the people, the animals, and the instruments of war. When he had loaded what he wished, he commanded the violent wind, and it came beneath that wooden platform and lifted it, until once it had risen with him, he commanded the gentle wind, and it carried him for a month in its evening journey and a month in its morning journey to wherever he wished. The gentle wind would pass over his army and over the field without stirring it, without raising dust, and without harming a bird. Wahb said: "It was related to me that at a dwelling by the bank of the Tigris, written in it [*kataba-hu*] [[omitted in manuscript A]] by one of Sulayman's companions, whether from the jinn or from humans: 'We alighted here, and we did not build what we found built. We set out in the morning from Istakhr, and we halted here, and we will set out from it, if Allah wills, and spend the night in al-Sham.'"

Muqatil said: The devils wove for Sulayman a carpet one farsakh by one farsakh, of gold woven into silk. A golden pulpit was set for him in the middle of the carpet, and he sat upon it. Around him were three thousand chairs of gold and silver. The prophets sat on the golden chairs and the scholars on the silver chairs, and around them were the people, and around the people were the jinn and the devils. The birds shaded him with their wings so that the sun did not touch him. The east wind lifted the carpet a distance of a month, from morning to afternoon and from afternoon to morning.

And on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Six hundred thousand chairs would be set out for Sulayman. The humans would sit nearest to him, then the jinn after them, then the birds would shade them, and then the wind would carry them.

al-Hasan said: When horses occupied the Prophet of Allah Sulayman, peace be upon him, until the afternoon prayer (*salat al-ʿasr*) passed him by, he became angry for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and he slaughtered the horses. Allah replaced them for him with something better than them. The fastest of the winds flowed by his command as he wished. He would set out in the morning from Iliya, take his midday rest at Istakhr, and then depart from it in the evening, so that his evening arrival would be at Babil.

Ibn Zayd said: He had a vessel of wood, and in it were a thousand corners, and in each corner a thousand chambers. The humans and jinn rode with him in it, and beneath each corner were a thousand devils who lifted that vessel. When it rose, the gentle wind came and carried it along with them. He would take his midday rest with a people between him and whom was a month's distance, and he would be in the evening with a people between him and whom was a month's distance. The people did not know until the armies had come upon them with him.

It is related that Sulayman journeyed from the land of Iraq in the morning and reached the city of Marw, and he prayed the afternoon prayer in the city of Balkh. The wind carried him and his armies, and the birds shaded them. Then he traveled from the city of Balkh, passing through the lands of the Turks, and then came to the lands of China, covering in the morning a distance of a month and in the afternoon the same. Then he turned to the right, away from the rising of the sun, along the shore of the sea, until he reached the land of Qandahar. He went out from it to the land of Makran and Kirman, then passed beyond them until he reached the land of Fars. He stayed there for days, set out from it in the morning, and halted at Kaskar. Then he departed for al-Sham, and his place of settlement was the city of Tadmur. Before his departure from al-Sham to Iraq, he had commanded the devils, and they built it for him with marble slabs, pillars, and white and yellow marble. The Nabigha said regarding this:

*Except Sulayman, when the King said to him:*
*"Rise up in the wilderness and mark out its boundaries [for the jinn]..."*

*And I have permitted the host of jinn*
*to build Tadmur with slabs and pillars.*

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 82–83 (part 1 of 3):

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And of the devils﴾, meaning: We subjected to him some of the devils, ﴿who dived for him﴾, meaning: they would enter beneath the water and bring forth for him jewels from the depths of the sea, ﴿and did other work besides that﴾, meaning: other than diving, which is what Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed of prayer niches and statues﴾ (Saba': 13), and so on.

﴿And We were watching over them﴾, so that they would not go out from His command. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "We kept them safe from spoiling what they had done." In the narrative, Sulayman, when he sent a devil with a man to do a task for him, would say to him: "If he finishes his work before night, keep him busy with another task so that he does not spoil what he has done." It was the habit of the devils that, when they finished their work and were not occupied with another task, they would destroy and spoil what they had done.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And Job, when he called out to his Lord﴾, meaning: he supplicated his Lord. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Job (peace be upon him) was a man from the Romans; he was Job son of Amos son of Razikh son of Rum son of Eis son of Isaac son of Abraham. His mother was from the descendants of Lot son of Haran. Allah had chosen him, made him a prophet, and spread the world out for him. He had al-BatanIyya in the land of Sham, all of it, its plains and its mountains, and he had in it every kind of wealth: cattle, camels, sheep, horses and donkeys, in a quantity and abundance that no other man could surpass. He had five hundred plows, each followed by five hundred servants, and every servant had a wife, a child and property. The equipment of each plow was carried by a she-ass that bore young, two, three, four, five or more. Allah, Exalted is He, had given him family and children, men and women. He was pious, righteous, merciful to the poor; he fed the needy, sponsored widows and orphans, honored the guest and gave to the wayfarer. He was grateful for Allah's blessings and fulfilled Allah's right. He was protected from the enemy of Allah, Iblis, from reaching him in the way he reaches the wealthy through heedlessness, negligence and being preoccupied with worldly things away from the command of Allah. He had three companions who believed in him and affirmed him: a man from the people of Yemen called Yaqin, and two men from one town, one of whom was called Yaldad and the other Safir. They were middle-aged. Iblis could not be barred from any of the heavens, and he would stand in them wherever he wished, until Allah raised Jesus, after which he was barred from four heavens. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, he was barred from the remaining three. Iblis heard the angels responding with prayers upon Job, at the time Allah mentioned him and praised him. Envy and resentment seized him, so he ascended swiftly until he stood at a place in the sky where he used to stand, and said: "My God, I considered the affair of Your servant Job and found him a servant whom You favored, and he thanked You; You granted him health and he praised You. If You were to test him by taking away what You gave him, he would change from his state of thankfulness and worship to You, and he would depart from Your obedience." Allah, Exalted is He, said: "Go, for I have given you power over his property." So the enemy of Allah, Iblis, swooped down until he landed on the earth. Then he gathered the ifrits of the jinn and the rebellious devils and said to them: "What strength do you have? For I have been given power over the property of Job." That is a dreadful calamity and a trial that men cannot endure.
