**Commentary of al-Baghawi (*Ma'alim al-Tanzil*) on Surah 21 (al-Anbiya'), verses 104–105:**

﴿On the Day We will roll up the heaven﴾. Abu Ja'far recited "tuṭwā" (*tuṭwá*) with a *tā'* and a *ḍammah* and a *fatḥah* on the *wāw*, with "al-samā'" (*al-samā'u*) in the nominative as the subject of the passive. The majority (*al-'āmmah*) recited with a *nūn* and a *fatḥah* on it and a *kasrah* on the *wāw*, with "al-samā'" (*al-samā'a*) in the accusative. ﴿Like the rolling of a scroll for writings﴾. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Ḥafṣ, from 'Āṣim, recited "lil-kutub" (*lil-kutubi*) in the plural. The others recited "lil-kitāb" (*lil-kitābi*) in the singular.

They differed concerning "al-sijill" (*al-sijillu*). Al-Suddī said: "al-sijill" is an angel who records the deeds of the servants, and the *lām* is superfluous, meaning "like the rolling of a scroll for writings," as in His saying ﴿It has drawn near to you﴾ (al-Naml: 72), where the *lām* is superfluous. Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid and most of the scholars said: "al-sijill" is the page (*al-ṣaḥīfah*) for writings, meaning because of what is written in it. The sense is "like the rolling of the page over what is written on it." "Al-sijill" is a noun derived from *al-musājalah*, which is correspondence (*al-mukātabah*). "Al-ṭayy" is the folding (*al-darj*), which is the opposite of unfolding (*al-nashr*).

﴿As We initiated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾, meaning: as We began you in your mothers' wombs barefoot, naked and uncircumcised (*ghurlan*), so We shall restore them on the Day of Resurrection. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ (al-An'ām: 94).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbās, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Indeed you will be gathered barefoot, naked and uncircumcised." Then he recited: ﴿As We initiated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾.[[Related by al-Bukhārī in *al-Anbiyā'*, chapter on the saying of God, exalted is He: "And God took Abraham as a close friend" (6/386); and by Muslim in *al-Jannah wa Ṣifat Na'īmihā*, chapter on the passing away of the world and the explanation of the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, no. 2860 (4/2194). The author also cites it in *Sharḥ al-Sunnah* (15/122–123).]] ﴿A promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doers﴾, meaning the restoration and the resurrection.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We had certainly written in the Psalms after the reminder﴾. Sa'īd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid said: "al-Zabūr" is all the revealed books, and "al-dhikr" is the Mother of the Book that is with Him. The meaning is: after He had written its mention in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*).

Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "al-Zabūr" is the Torah, and "al-dhikr" is the books revealed after the Torah.

Al-Sha'bī said: "al-Zabūr" is the Book of David, [and "al-dhikr" is the Torah. It was also said: "al-Zabūr" is the Psalms of David,] [[What is between the brackets is an addition from manuscript "B".]] and "al-dhikr" is the Qur'an. "Ba'd" here means "qabl" (before), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there was behind them a king﴾ (al-Kahf: 79), meaning "in front of them." And ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾ (al-Nāzi'āt: 30), meaning "before that."

﴿That the earth﴾, meaning the earth of Paradise, ﴿My righteous servants will inherit﴾. Mujāhid said: meaning the community of Muhammad ﷺ. Its proof is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us and given us the earth as an inheritance"﴾ (al-Zumar: 74).

Ibn 'Abbās said: he meant that the lands of the disbelievers will be conquered by the Muslims, and this is a ruling from God to make the religion prevail and to strengthen the Muslims. It was also said: by "the earth" he meant the Holy Land (*al-arḍ al-muqaddasah*).

**Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 21, verses 106–109:**

﴿Indeed, in this﴾, i.e., in this Qur'an, ﴿is a message﴾, meaning arrival at the desired goal. That is, whoever follows the Qur'an and acts upon it reaches what he hopes for of reward. It was also said: "a message" means sufficiency. It is said, "In this thing there is *balagh* and *balaghah*," meaning sufficiency, and the Qur'an is the provision for Paradise, like the provision (*balagh*) of the traveler. ﴿For a people who worship﴾, i.e., the believers who worship Allah. Ibn Abbas said: "those who have knowledge." **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 110–112:**

﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud, and He knows what you conceal.﴾

﴿And I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾ That is, perhaps the delay of the punishment from you is a metaphor for something not mentioned, ﴿a trial﴾ meaning a test, ﴿for you﴾ so that He may see how you act, although He is most knowing, ﴿and a provision for a time﴾ meaning you enjoy (worldly provision) until the end of your appointed terms.

﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, recited: ﴿Qala rabbi uhkum﴾ ("He said: My Lord, judge"), while the others read: "Qul rabbi uhkum" ("Say: My Lord, judge"). The meaning is: separate me and those who denied me with truth. If it is asked, "How can He say judge with truth, when Allah judges only with truth?" It is answered: the truth here means the punishment, as if he were asking for the punishment to befall his people, and so they were punished on the Day of Badr. A parallel to this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ (al-Aʿraf: 89). The scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani) said: its meaning is "My Lord, judge with Your true judgment," so the word "judgment" is omitted and "truth" is put in its place. Allah the Exalted judges with truth whether or not He is asked, and the meaning of "asking" is the manifestation of the desire of the one asking for His true judgment.

﴿And our Lord is the Most Merciful, whose help is sought against what you describe﴾ of lies and falsehood.
